summary: Describes the commonly used Base64, Base32, and Base16 encodings, and discusses line feeds, padding, characters outside the alphabet, and different alphabets. It is informational and was replaced by RFC 4648.

eli5.summary: Computers can turn any file into plain letters and numbers so it survives a trip through systems meant only for text. This memo explains those ways of writing data.

questions: when should i use base64 vs base32
subtitle: Three ways to turn binary data into safe text.

tldr.problem: Applications need to send binary data through systems that only handle text, like email or URLs. Binary data can get corrupted or rejected when sent through text-only channels.
tldr.mechanism: Base encoding represents binary data using only safe printable characters. Base64 uses 64 characters (including A-Z, a-z, 0-9, +, /), Base32 uses 32 characters (A-Z, 2-7), and Base16 uses 16 characters (0-9, A-F).
tldr.outcome: Any binary data can be safely transmitted through text-only systems. The data grows larger (Base64 by about 33%), but is recoverable. RFC 4648 later unified and refined these standards.

today: RFC 3548 is Informational and was obsoleted by RFC 4648 in October 2006, which clarified these encodings further and became the standard reference.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Base encoding lets programs store or send binary data (any kind of file) through systems that only understand text. These systems often have historical reasons for being text-only, such as email, which was designed to carry ASCII characters.

Without a standard way to encode binary data, different applications created slightly different encoding schemes. This RFC documents the three most common encodings—Base64, Base32, and Base16—and establishes rules to ensure they all work the same way everywhere.
sections.eli5: Encoding is like writing a picture as a story so you can send it through a telephone system that only handles words.

sections.title: The Three Encoding Schemes
sections.content:
Base64 is the most common. It uses a 65-character alphabet: uppercase letters (A-Z), lowercase letters (a-z), digits (0-9), plus (+), and slash (/), plus an equals sign (=) for padding. Each character represents 6 bits of data. Three bytes of input (24 bits) become four Base64 characters.

Base32 uses a 33-character alphabet: uppercase letters (A-Z) and digits (2-7), plus equals signs for padding. Each character represents 5 bits. Five bytes of input (40 bits) become eight Base32 characters. Base32 is case-insensitive, making it useful where case might not be preserved.

Base16 (hexadecimal) uses 16 characters: digits (0-9) and letters (A-F). Each character represents 4 bits. One byte of input becomes two Base16 characters. Base16 does not require padding.
sections.eli5: Base64 is like a code where each symbol is worth 6 bits. Base32 is like a code where each symbol is worth 5 bits. Base16 (hex) is like a code where each symbol is worth 4 bits.

sections.title: Encoding Process and Padding
sections.content:
Encoding breaks the input into fixed-size chunks. For Base64, three input bytes (24 bits) are split into four 6-bit groups. Each group becomes one Base64 character. If the last chunk has fewer than three bytes, zero bits are added on the right, and the output is padded with equals signs (=) so the total length is always a multiple of 4.

For Base32, five input bytes (40 bits) become eight 5-bit groups. Padding with equals signs makes the output length a multiple of 8. Base16 needs no padding because a byte always divides evenly into two 4-bit groups.

Implementations MUST include padding unless a specification explicitly says otherwise. This ensures decoders can always recover the exact original data.
sections.eli5: Encoding takes a number of bits, divides them into chunks, and turns each chunk into a safe character. If the last chunk is too small, padding characters are added.

sections.title: Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
Implementations face several common decisions. Line length: MIME email adds line breaks after 76 Base64 characters, but this RFC says encoders MUST NOT add line breaks unless the specification explicitly says to do so. Character interpretation: Decoders MUST reject any characters outside the defined alphabet, unless the specification says otherwise (as MIME does).

Alphabet choice: Base64 uses + and / as characters 62 and 63. However, these characters are problematic in URLs and filenames. A URL-safe variant substitutes - (minus) and _ (underscore) instead. The RFC documents both alphabets to reduce ambiguity.

Base16 and Base32 can be uppercase or lowercase; implementations may handle either or both, but MUST NOT silently accept out-of-alphabet characters without being explicitly told to.
sections.eli5: When you encode, don't break the text into lines unless told to. When you decode, reject anything that is not a safe character. Different alphabets work for different situations.

sections.title: Security and Limitations
sections.content:
Base encoding is visual obfuscation, not encryption. A password encoded in Base64 looks like random text but is trivial to decode. This false sense of confidentiality has caused security incidents when people thought encoded passwords were protected.

Decoders must be careful to avoid buffer overflows and to reject invalid input correctly. If a decoder ignores non-alphabet characters instead of rejecting them, an attacker could use that difference as a covert channel to send hidden information. When Base16 and Base32 are case-insensitive, case changes themselves can be used to leak information.

The primary purpose of base encoding is to make data compatible with text-only systems, not to protect it.
sections.eli5: Encoding makes data look like random letters, but anyone can decode it with a few seconds of work. Encoding is not the same as locking it with a key.
